title: Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit
summary: Bootkit is the Pre-OS Boot sub-technique in which malicious code is planted in the boot path on disk so that it executes before the operating system takes control. The parent category covers pre boot persistence in general and System Firmware covers the mainboard; a bootkit instead lives on storage, where an attacker with raw disk access can divert startup execution. On older BIOS style systems this means overwriting the master boot record, the first sector the firmware loads and the home of the boot loader, or the volume boot record that the master boot record passes control to. On UEFI systems the equivalent move is to create or modify files in the EFI system partition, the small dedicated partition that holds boot loaders and utilities, allowing the attacker to load kernel code or a signed component that the platform already trusts. Because execution begins before operating system security features exist, a bootkit can hide itself, subvert the kernel or re establish malicious components after a conventional clean up, and it typically also writes the boot area, which produces disk level artefacts such as changed boot sector contents, altered partition entries and unexpected new or modified files in the system partition. Comparing boot code and partition structures against a known good baseline, and using measured boot or secure boot verification, is the practical way to spot the difference.

beginner.definition: A bootkit is malicious code that hides in the area of the disk used to start the computer. It runs before the operating system loads. The word kit here means a set of malicious tools packaged together.
beginner.whyItMatters: It runs first, so it can hide from everything that starts later. Removing normal malware may not remove it. It can bring other malicious files back after a clean up. It may also stop you from trusting anything the machine reports.
howItWorks: The parent topic covers pre boot attacks in general. A bootkit specifically alters the parts of the disk used during startup.
The attacker needs raw access to the disk. Raw access means writing to the disk directly, without normal file rules.
On older systems they overwrite the master boot record, the first disk block, or the volume boot record after it.
On modern systems they may instead change or add files in the small special partition that holds the boot loader.
When the machine starts, the changed boot code loads first and can interfere with the operating system kernel.
The boot area is small and rarely changes, so defenders compare it with a trusted copy to find the difference.
beginner.example: Think of a shop that keeps its opening checklist in a tray by the front door. Someone swaps that checklist for a fake one. Every morning the staff follow the fake list, unlock the wrong door and write the wrong alarm code, long before the manager arrives.
takeaways: Bootkits live on disk but run before the operating system, so normal clean up may not remove them.
Trust measurements of boot code and partition layout, taken before an infection, to spot changes later.
Suspect a bootkit when malware reappears after a rebuild, and treat protection features as unreliable on that host.

objectives: Define a bootkit and explain how it differs from the parent Pre-OS Boot category and from firmware tampering.
Name the disk areas a bootkit modifies on BIOS style and on UEFI systems.
Explain why effective removal requires more than deleting ordinary malicious files.
Describe how measured boot and secure boot verification help reveal a modified boot path.
Explain why an infected host's own reporting cannot be fully trusted during investigation.
